reviews.reason: Emperor Wu to whom Yang Hu recommended Lü in this chapter (Western Jin context). Same-title Emperor Wu at s0065 is a separate local/canonical record (jinshu:093:p034); equivalence is not merged here and stays uncertain. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.

Jia Chong named in the historian's preface as an in-law already given his own biography; chapter attribution as a mention is correct. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.

Courtesy name 弘理 in the closing appraisal refers to Du Yi (s0104 杜乂，字弘理). This record covers only the appraisal mention; the s0104 biography subject is not in this case, so same-chapter equivalence stays unresolved and is not merged here. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.
Second son Rong, Grand Minister of Agriculture in the Yuanxi era, in the He Zhun family section. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.
Yu Liang (courtesy name 元規 at s0020) named in the preface as an eminent in-law; also listed at s0022. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.
Wang Xiu, son of Wang Meng (s0216 有二子：修、蘊), courtesy name Jingren, childhood name Gouzi. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.

Xun Fengqian, used as a comparison for Liu Tan; a mention only, not an actor in this chapter. Cross-record equivalence is uncertain. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.
Xie An praising Wang Meng; he also speaks at s0245. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.

Yang Hu, South-Pacifying General, who recommended Lü to Emperor Wu. The anchor is the abbreviated 羊 in the pair 羊、杜 (Yang Hu and Du Yu as model generals). Identifying it as Yang Hu is a standard allusion but rests only on a single-character reference, so cross-chapter equivalence stays explicitly uncertain. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.

Chu Pou as grandfather of Chu Shuang (s0269), Lord Chu at s0245 and 季野 at s0276. Same-chapter local records jinshu:093:p084 and jinshu:093:p015 sit under different canonical IDs; they are not merged here and stay unresolved. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.

Chu Pou by his courtesy name (s0116 褚裒，字季野) in the preface. Duplicate canonical records exist for p084 and p150; they are not merged here. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.

Emperor Wu, who banned the recruiting of clients during Wang Xun's tenure (Western Jin). Whether this is the same person as p076 is not merged here and stays uncertain. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.
Chu Xiuzhi, son of Chu Shuang, who held high office in the Yixi era. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.

Chu Pou as the biography subject (visits Yu Liang as a boy; the northern campaign at s0156). Duplicate canonical records exist for p015 and p150; they are not merged here. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.

Wang Meng, father of Wang Yun; also 亡祖長史 at s0263 and 仲祖 at s0276. His own biography opens at s0185 (王濛，字仲祖); same-chapter equivalence with that subject is not merged here. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.

Mi Yi, an army inspector sent by Chu Pou who advanced to Xiapi and held the city. One clear actor in one chapter. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.
Lady Pei, Du Yi's widow, who raised Empress Chenggong. Titled 高安鄉君 at s0111 and 廣德縣君 at s0112. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.

王叔仁 is the courtesy name of Wang Yun (s0230 王蘊，字叔仁), who asked to be sent out to a command. The local record's personal-name claim "Wang Shu" (c0047) and the s0021 English "Wang Shu" are wrong: Wang Shu (述) is a different man (s0223). Held until the name is corrected; the referent itself is attested.
Yang Dan, father of Yang Xiu (s0023), Grand Master of Ceremonies. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.
Emperor Jianwen, at that time Prince of Kuaiji serving as regent; 簡文皇帝 at s0263. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.
Yin Hao, Palace Attendant, recommended by Chu Pou; 浩 at s0153. Accepted membership is consistent with the cited source; no wrong actor or false merge found.

supplementalEditorialRepairs.before: Chu Pou shrank from wielding power at court, and Wang Shu begged to be sent to the frontier; both kept their skins and their honor, and deserve mention.
supplementalEditorialRepairs.after: Chu Pou shrank from wielding power at court, and Wang Yun begged to be sent to the frontier; both kept their skins and their honor, and deserve mention.
supplementalEditorialRepairs.sourceBasedReason: 王叔仁 is the courtesy name of Wang Yun (s0230 王蘊，字叔仁). "Wang Shu" wrongly names him and could be confused with Wang Shu 述 (s0223).
supplementalEditorialRepairs.pairedFieldChecked: As for Chu Yeye’s fearing and avoiding court power, and Wang Shuren’s firmly seeking to go out and hold a command, by this they were able to preserve the body and keep far from harm—there is something to praise in that.
